name: Gareth Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I translate technical documents from French into English, freelance, from a desk in my flat above a bakery. Mostly it's manuals for industrial pumps and valves, safety sheets, the odd patent. I start at eight with coffee and a translation memory program I've used for six years, which remembers my old sentences, and I work through until about five. I like the quiet and the precision, and what wears me out is invoicing and chasing payment.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: One pump manufacturer, Kessler, gives me about half my work, which is too much from one place, I know. The rest comes through two agencies. I've never used the AI translation tools, I don't trust them with torque values and warning labels. My uncle Imran keeps saying I should have been an electrician like him, and some months I think he's right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it was always going to be overhyped. I'm not really one for posting, but at the pub I'd say the people who panicked look a bit silly now. Then I'd probably change the subject to football.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm still not comfortable. Kessler started trialling a machine translation system last spring for their simpler manuals, and even a so-so tool is good enough for a parts list. Half my income from one client is a risk with or without AI, and I've got about four months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am, because it's what I know. I'd try to get one more steady client through the agencies so Kessler isn't half my income, and I'd stop buying takeaways during the week. I'd put the difference into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit tense, honestly. The same feeling as now, really, which isn't great.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if Kessler cuts back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I lose half my work overnight and I've got four months to replace it. Kessler (the pump maker that gives me half my work) only needs a cheap tool to be good enough for parts lists, not brilliant. That's the bit people miss when they say AI is hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably nobody, if I'm honest. Maybe my uncle Imran over Sunday lunch, and he'd just say electrician again. I tend to keep things to myself until I've sorted them.

say: The AI talk was **always overhyped**, and the panickers look a bit silly now.
I'd **rather talk football** than argue about technology at the pub.
think: **Kessler's machine translation** trial threatens my simpler manual work even without big AI.
Having **half my income** from one client is risky with only four months saved.
do: **Carry on** with his translation memory program and the same routine.
**Look for another** steady agency client to reduce reliance on Kessler.
**Stop weekday takeaways** and save the difference.
feel: **Tense**, the same background worry he already lives with.
S0.quote: Kessler (the pump maker that gives me half my work) only needs a cheap tool to be good enough for parts lists, not brilliant.
fieldNote: His worry comes from **one big client**, not from AI itself.
Publicly **shrugs it off**, privately counts his months of savings.
**Keeps problems to himself**, which may slow any response.

steps.text: Keep translating pump manuals with the same memory program
Ask both agencies for one more steady technical client
Drop weekday takeaways and bank the savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's just how markets work, and every job changes. I wouldn't make a fuss about it publicly. If someone asked, I'd say technical translation still needs a human to sign off on safety stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm in real trouble. Manuals and safety sheets are exactly the sort of writing and checking this picture says goes first. Kessler would put everything through software and pay someone to glance over it, and that someone might not be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold on with Kessler as long as they'd have me, even at lower checking rates. I'd ring my uncle Imran about the electrician apprenticeship he keeps mentioning, and actually ask how it works this time. And I'd cut down to essentials, no holiday this year, and get savings up toward six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sinking. Like I've been ignoring something for a while and it's caught up with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've never used the AI tools. Would you learn them now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to try, but I'd be slow at it and I know that. The younger translators at the agency would be quicker. It's not that I can't learn, I just don't like it, and that matters more than people think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would an apprenticeship mean for your money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd be a big drop, maybe half what I earn now for a couple of years. I'd probably have to give up the flat and move back into my mum's spare room. At twenty-seven, moving back home to train as an electrician isn't the life I pictured.

say: It's just **how markets work**, and every job changes.
Technical translation still needs a human to **sign off** on safety documents.
think: Manuals and safety sheets are exactly the **writing and checking** that goes first.
Kessler would pay someone to **glance over software output**, maybe not me.
do: **Hold on with Kessler** even at lower checking rates.
**Call his uncle** about how an electrician apprenticeship actually works.
**Cut to essentials**, skip the holiday and push savings toward six months.
feel: **Sinking**, as if an ignored problem has finally caught up.
S1.quote: At twenty-seven, moving back home to train as an electrician isn't the life I pictured.
fieldNote: Calm public line, but privately he expects to **lose most work**.
**Resistant to the tools** because he dislikes them, not because he can't learn.
The **electrician route** is a family nudge he has resisted for years.

steps.text: Accept lower checking rates to keep Kessler work
Ask his uncle about starting an electrician apprenticeship
Skip this year's holiday and cut to essentials
Push savings toward six months of costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say not much at all, honestly. Maybe that it's happening too fast and nobody's in charge. If pressed, I'd say I'm looking at other options, which sounds better than it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think translation's finished for me by 2028. It's all screen work, so it goes right on the date. The one useful thing is the three-year gap before robots do hands-on work, which is roughly how long an electrician apprenticeship takes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the apprenticeship as soon as my uncle Imran could get me in, in the first year. I'd give up the flat and move into my mum's spare room to make the money last. I'd do whatever translation checking I could on evenings and weekends until it dried up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, and a bit numb. I'd be doing things before I'd really felt them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You pointed out the three-year gap. Does that make the apprenticeship a safe bet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not safe, but less bad. If robots arrive around 2031, I'd only just be qualified as an electrician. I'd be betting that rewiring old houses is messy enough that robots take a while longer still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your mum say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be pleased to have me home and worried at the same time. She'd say she always knew the computer job wasn't real work. My mum means well, but that sort of thing stings.

say: It's happening **too fast**, and nobody's in charge.
I'm **looking at other options**, which sounds better than it is.
think: Translation is **finished by 2028**, because it's all screen work.
The **three-year robot gap** matches an electrician apprenticeship almost exactly.
do: **Start the apprenticeship** through his uncle in the first year.
**Give up the flat** and move into his mum's spare room.
**Take any checking work** on evenings and weekends until it dries up.
feel: **Alarmed and numb**, acting before he has really felt it.
S2.quote: If robots arrive around 2031, I'd only just be qualified as an electrician.
fieldNote: He used the **robot delay** sharply: it's the window for a hands-on trade.
Moving home is the **cost-cutting move**, and it hurts his pride.
Very **little public voice**; he deals with things privately.

steps.text: Start an electrician apprenticeship through his uncle Imran
Give up the flat above the bakery
Move into his mum's spare room to stretch savings
Take evening and weekend checking work while it lasts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is fair warning and anyone sensible will use it. I'd probably say that to my mates and leave it there. I'm not going to march about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it still means translation ends for me, around 2031. But five years means I could plan the switch instead of being shoved. I'd be thirty-two, which is late for an apprentice but not ridiculous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep translating for the first year or two and save hard, aiming for a year of costs. Then I'd start the apprenticeship in year two or three, ideally while keeping a few days of checking work. I'd ask Kessler if they'd give me a reference for technical roles, maybe pump servicing, which is closer to hands-on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but less trapped. More like a bad forecast than a storm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Pump servicing is an interesting idea. Where did that come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know those pumps inside out from translating the manuals. I could probably name every seal in a Kessler centrifugal pump. If Kessler took me on as a service technician, that's six years of manuals finally paying off in a different way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the AI tools at all, with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably for the checking work in the first year, because it'd be the only work going. I wouldn't enjoy it. But I'd rather be paid to check a machine than not paid at all.

say: **Five years** is fair warning, and anyone sensible will use it.
I'm **not going to march** about it; I'll just get on with planning.
think: Five years lets me **plan the switch** at thirty-two instead of being shoved.
do: **Save hard** for a year of costs while still translating.
**Start an apprenticeship** in year two or three, keeping some checking days.
**Ask Kessler** for a reference toward pump servicing roles.
feel: **Worried but less trapped**, like a bad forecast rather than a storm.
S3.quote: I could probably name every seal in a Kessler centrifugal pump.
fieldNote: He still **expects to lose** his job, so the mood stays alarmed.
Finds a **creative bridge**: translation knowledge into pump servicing.
Would **grudgingly use AI** only when it's the only paid work left.

steps.text: Save toward a full year of living costs
Begin an electrician apprenticeship in year two or three
Ask Kessler about a pump service technician role
Use AI tools for paid checking work in year one

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and lots can happen. I'd probably tell people not to get carried away. I'd keep my head down and work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years means I'd probably get most of a decade translating, which is a relief. But it ends in the same place. The danger for someone like me is I'd put it off, because I always do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on translating, and try to spread my work so Kessler isn't half of it. In year two or three I'd do an evening course in electrical installation, just the first level, so it's there if I need it. And I'd keep adding to savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but with a nagging feeling. Like a dentist appointment I know I'll eventually have to book.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put it off. What would make you actually start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kessler cutting my rate, probably. When Kessler (the pump maker that sends me half my work) cuts my rate, I'll stop dithering and book the electrician course that week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the ten years change anything in your personal life?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd stop renting and buy somewhere small, because I'd have years of steady income. But I'd want the electrical course started first. I'm not signing a twenty-five-year mortgage on a job that ends in ten.

say: **Ten years** is a long time, and lots can happen.
People shouldn't **get carried away**; I'd keep my head down and work.
think: I'd likely get **most of a decade** translating, which is a relief.
The danger is I'd **put it off**, because I always do.
do: **Spread his work** so Kessler is no longer half his income.
**Take a first-level** electrical installation course in the evenings around year two.
feel: **Calmer**, with a nagging feeling, like a dentist appointment still to book.
S4.quote: I'm not signing a twenty-five-year mortgage on a job that ends in ten.
fieldNote: **Procrastination** is his biggest risk, and he knows it.
Uses a **rate cut from Kessler** as his trigger to act.
Still expects the **job to end**, so anxious rather than uneasy.

steps.text: Win more agency work so Kessler drops below half his income
Take a first-level evening electrical course around year two
Delay buying a flat until the electrical course is started

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It's the only one where I don't have time to get a trade before both the translating and the hands-on work get hit. What would help is a properly paid apprenticeship for people my age, not just school leavers, so I don't have to move back in with my mum.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about people who work alone. I don't have colleagues to compare notes with. Working alone in a flat above a bakery, you only find out the world's changed when the emails stop.

headlineQuote: Working alone in a flat above a bakery, you only find out the world's changed when the emails stop.
portrait: A **27-year-old freelance** French to English technical translator who relies on one pump maker.
**Never uses AI tools**, preferring his translation memory program and quiet routine.
Already **anxious** about **one big client**, even if AI goes nowhere.
Sees an **electrician apprenticeship** as his way out, timed to the robot delay.
Keeps worries **to himself** and admits he tends to put things off.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, leaving no time to learn a trade before robots arrive.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid apprenticeship** for people his age, so he needn't move back home.
